opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that Kaiming has an almost unusual sense for what is *simple* and what is *fundamental*. A lot of people in our field are good at making things work, adding modules and tricks until the number goes up. Kaiming tends to go the other way. He asks: what is the one essential thing here, and can I strip everything else away? ResNet is a good example. The residual connection is almost embarrassingly simple, but it addressed a real, fundamental problem in optimization, and that's why it lasted.

The second thing is that he's very patient and very honest with himself. When I worked with him, what struck me was that he doesn't get excited by a result just because it looks good. He wants to understand *why* it works. He'll run the ablation everyone else skips, he'll check whether the baseline was actually tuned properly. In a field moving this fast, that discipline is rare, and it's part of why his papers are so trustworthy. People can build on them.

Third, he has a good sense of timing, of what problem the community is ready for. He doesn't chase every trend, but when he picks a direction, like masked autoencoders for vision, it's usually because he sees that the conditions have changed and an old idea can now really work. It's not just taste in ideas, it's taste in *when*.

And honestly, I think a big part of it is that he really cares about the writing and the presentation. A Kaiming paper reads very clean. Every figure has a purpose. That clarity isn't separate from the research taste. It reflects how clearly he thinks about the problem in the first place.

So if I had to summarize: simplicity, rigor, timing, and clarity. Many people have one or two of these. He's unusual in that he has all of them at the same time, and has kept them consistently for so many years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is that Kaiming is extremely good at asking the simplest possible version of a question. A lot of people, when they see a problem, immediately start adding things, more modules, more tricks, more terms in the loss. Kaiming does the opposite. He keeps stripping things away until what's left is almost embarrassingly simple, and then he asks, why doesn't this already work? ResNet is the obvious example. The question wasn't "how do we build a fancier network," it was "why does a deeper network do worse than a shallower one, when in principle it could just learn identity?" Once you frame it that way, the residual connection almost falls out. MAE is the same story. People had been trying masked image modeling for years with complicated designs, and he basically said, what if we just mask a lot, like 75 percent, and use a plain autoencoder? Everyone assumed that was too naive.

The second thing is that he is relentless about understanding, not just about numbers. When I worked with him, we'd have a result that was good, and most people would move on to writing the paper. He would keep running ablations, not to pad the paper, but because he genuinely wanted to know which part actually mattered. He's not satisfied when something works. He wants to know why it works, and if he can't explain it in one or two sentences, he doesn't fully trust it. That discipline is where a lot of the taste comes from, because over time you build an intuition for what's real signal and what's noise.

And the third thing, honestly, is patience and a kind of indifference to trends. He's not chasing whatever is hot this quarter. He thinks about what the field will need in three to five years, and he's willing to work on something unfashionable if he believes the question is fundamental. That combination of simplicity, insistence on understanding, and a long time horizon is pretty rare. I learned a lot from just watching how he said no to ideas, actually. Most of taste is knowing what not to do.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is his ability to identify the core problem. In research, you can have a system with ten things going on, and it’s tempting to add an eleventh thing to make it work better. The harder question is: which of those ten things actually matters? Can we make the problem simpler and understand it more clearly?

That’s the quality I associate with Kaiming’s research taste. It’s not just a preference for simple methods. A simple method can be trivial, too. The skill is finding a simplification that reveals something important—something that changes how you think about the problem.

And I think that requires patience and independent judgment. You have to be willing to sit with a basic question, even when everyone else is moving toward something more complicated. The final result may look obvious, but recognizing which question is worth pursuing is the difficult part.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is his ability to identify the core question. There are always many things you can try, and many ways to make a system more complicated. The difficult thing is figuring out which part actually matters.

The taste I associate with Kaiming is a preference for simple ideas that reveal something fundamental. That doesn’t mean the work is easy. Often, getting to a clean explanation requires a lot of careful experimentation. But the result feels inevitable once you understand it.

And he seems willing to question assumptions that everyone else has stopped noticing. To me, that combination—asking a basic question and pursuing it very rigorously—is what makes his research taste so strong.
